classification.difficultyReason: Parts a and b scaffold finding half of 6 and a third of 12. The student compares the shaded counts, then explains why 1/3 of a larger whole can exceed 1/2 of a smaller one. That final part needs an interpretation of fractions against unequal wholes, supported by the earlier results. It is more reasoning than routine comparison, but far less open than p43-q6, which requires the same insight with less scaffolding.

content.prompt: Rectangle A has $\frac12$ shaded and rectangle B has $\frac13$ shaded.

children.label: a
children.prompt: How many squares are shaded in rectangle A?

answer.worked:
Rectangle A has 6 squares and half are shaded.
$$\begin{align*}6\div2&=3\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: How many squares are shaded in rectangle B?

answer.worked:
Rectangle B has 12 squares and a third are shaded.
$$\begin{align*}12\div3&=4\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Which rectangle has the larger shaded area?

answer.worked: B has 4 shaded squares and A has 3 shaded squares, so B has the larger shaded area.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Does this mean $\frac13$ is greater than $\frac12$? Explain.

answer.short: No. $\frac13<\frac12$, but B is a larger whole than A.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\frac12&=\frac36\\\frac13&=\frac26\end{align*}$$
So $\frac13<\frac12$. Rectangle B has 12 squares and rectangle A has 6 squares, so a smaller fraction of the larger whole can still be a larger area.
